author: leesec
cardQuote: As someone working in automotive-tech, this company is still vaporware in my mind.
quote: As someone working in automotive-tech, this company is still vaporware in my mind. I hope it is a success as I am a fan of EV's but until I see a single Rivian doing anything I'd be very skeptical of a 2021 release date. Would also probably be willing to bet more than 100k Rivian vehicles never get produced.
outcome: Rivian shipped the R1T in 2021 and went public at a valuation just under $100 billion.
outcomeDetail: Rivian began R1T deliveries in September 2021 and listed on Nasdaq in November 2021 at $100.73 a share, briefly valuing it above GM and Ford. Amazon ordered 100,000 electric delivery vans, and Rivian has produced well over 100,000 vehicles.
note: leesec was right that Rivian missed its original 2021 timing, but wrong that it was vaporware: it became one of the best-funded EV startups and actually shipped.

author: JanSolo
cardQuote: They've been working for over 10 years on this and shown almost nothing.
quote: Finally something concrete from these guys! They've been working for over 10 years on this and shown almost nothing. The capsule looks nice; big curved windows and no RCS thrusters tell us that this is not an orbital capsule. The 1st Stage reuse concept is interesting; the ducting near the capsule connector is quite novel. There are 8 large spoilers that protrude into the airflow to help slow descent. I wonder if these can be modulated to give some kind of stability control? It's interesting to note that although the capsule landed successfully, they make no mention of what happened to the launcher. I presume that it failed to land, but I didn't see any smoking wreckage in the background of the capsule landing video, so maybe it made it down in 1 piece? I'm sure they would have told us if it had. Anyway, a good day for the US space industry; Blue Origin finally have something cool to show and have proved that they're not just purveyors of vaporware. I'm looking forward to seeing what else they can come up with.
storyTitle: Blue Origin: Images and Videos from Our First Flight
outcome: Blue Origin reached orbit with New Glenn in January 2025 and landed its booster in November 2025.
outcomeDetail: After years of suborbital New Shepard flights, Blue Origin's New Glenn reached orbit on its first launch in January 2025. In November 2025 the company landed a New Glenn booster at sea, becoming the second company to do so.
note: In 2015 the company had flown only suborbital test hops, so the impatience was fair. But 'shown almost nothing' aged badly once New Glenn reached orbit and landed.

author: rebootthesystem
cardQuote: Lucid Motors has been blabbering incessantly about a car for quite some time now.
quote: I continue to be astounded to see companies chase each other off the cliff repeating one of the most destructive marketing techniques ever invented: Promoting imaginary non-existing products. "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in FOUR YEARS". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in THREE YEARS". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in TWO YEARS". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in ONE YEAR". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in TWO YEARS". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in THREE YEARS". "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in... Shit! We have no buyers". People want to solve problems today. They don't go to Home Depot to buy a drill bit for a hole they need to drill in four years. Or two. They need to drill a hole now. The constant announcement of vapor products only serves to either tell the audience you are clueless and have no product anywhere near a reasonable horizon or --not sure which is worst-- push people into making a decision in favor of a competitor. Cars are a displacement market. This is a market where a purchasing decision means a long term loss of the opportunity by all competitors. Once someone buys a car they stop looking for 2 to 10 years. In a displacement market, spooking your prospects into making a decision in favor of a competitor generally means you slit your own throat. You thought you were being hip and cool while making amazing advanced announcements of a vapor product and, instead, you convinced prospects that you and your product are not real. The next move is natural: If they have a reasonably immediate need they lose all trust and hope on you and buy the competitor's product. See you in a decade. This, BTW, is very common in engineer-driven companies. I know. I was the moron making these incredibly dumb decisions for my own business twenty years ago. I can't even described the amount of business I lost because I convinced myself that talking about what's coming "real soon" was actually of interest to my prospects. It wasn't. They bought the competitor's product and I lost them for a decade or for a lifetime. They got tired of hearing me go on about a nonexistent mythical product. Some of these losses represented company-changing multi-million-dollar multi-year lifetime opportunities. Gone. Shitty way to learn a lesson. It's a very different thing if a company like BMW says "We are building a pure electric and here's the i3 and i8, two of our experiments" vs. a Joe-Blow-Startup without a factory or scale saying "...coming soon". BMW can survive this because it has a reputation and a following. Some people (my wife) would rather buy an electric BMW to replace her current IC BMW. She is happy to wait. She trusts and likes BWM and knows they can deliver. She likes Tesla, but BWM saying "we are almost there" along with their reputation is likely to keep her from buying a Tesla. On the other hand such loyalty does not exist with an unknown startup. The effect is to eventually see the continuing announcements of vapor as a signal that they are never going to be a viable option. And they are gone. OK smart-ass. How do you do it then? Simple. Develop a product. Finish it. Get it to the point where you can deliver a good reliable product. At that point, not before, announce it and open the doors. As much fanfare as you want. Market as far and wide as your budget and skills allow. The key is: The product has to be real and you have to be able to take orders AND deliver now, not in two years. Lucid Motors has been blabbering incessantly about a car for quite some time now. And their "important announcement" is: "Look at us! We are going to have THIS disruptive product in TWO YEARS". Yeah. Good luck. Shitty way to learn a lesson.
storyTitle: Lucid Motors unveils the Air, a new luxe electric car with a 400-mile range
outcome: Lucid delivered the Air in 2021 with a 520-mile EPA range and went public at a $24 billion valuation.
outcomeDetail: The Air entered production in September 2021, and the top version received a 520-mile EPA rating. Lucid merged with Churchill Capital IV in July 2021 at a $24 billion valuation, backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. Volume remained far below early promises.
note: The car arrived roughly five years after the 2016 unveiling, so the timing criticism was fair. The 'vaporware' framing was not: Lucid shipped a record-range sedan and became a public company.

author: Animats
cardQuote: The number of "it's going to be really cheap" battery claims far exceeds the number of really cheap and usable batteries that actually ship.
quote: > Also, people in that industry know that surely no one would proudly advertise a "100 hour battery" if it weren't significantly cheaper than lithium ion on a per kWh basis Or they just have a slow-discharge technology and are trying to create the illusion it's good for something. > at less than 1/10th the cost of lithium-ion That's just a PR statement at this point. They haven't built many batteries. If the materials cost for a lithium-ion battery went down 90%, battery cost would only go down 50%.[1] The number of "it's going to be really cheap" battery claims far exceeds the number of really cheap and usable batteries that actually ship. [1] https://qnovo.com/82-the-cost-components-of-a-battery
storyTitle: Form Energy reveals the chemistry of its long-duration battery
outcome: Form Energy built its West Virginia factory and signed a 30 GWh, $1 billion supply deal with Google in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Form Energy moved its iron-air batteries from pilot lines to a $760 million factory in Weirton, West Virginia. In 2026 Google contracted for a 300 MW/30 GWh system, and Crusoe signed a further 12 GWh agreement. The company has raised more than $1 billion.
note: Animats was right that battery startups overpromise cheap cells, but Form Energy actually reached commercial offtake and manufacturing. The 'PR statement' became a signed Google deal.

author: actionberries
cardQuote: The chances of this company becoming a unicorn must be vanishingly small.
quote: Because SpaceX is known to over-promise and under-deliver? They seem to have an extremely powerful institutional engineering capability. That's not fanboy talk e.g., we're going to mars! Just look at what they've accomplished. Landing a rocket on its business end is no mean feat -- for any engineering team, ever. I know this is a YC forum but seeing the Astranis team's responses to people asking very incisive questions is troubling. Maybe they're far better at engineering than building confidence but I detect that sort of single minded dismissal (often of objective reality) that plagues a lot of entrepreneurs. Maybe this is unfair but it sounds like someone got latched onto the idea of "micro-satellites" and won't let it go, ending up with "we can conceivably put up only X, so they'd have to be geosynchronous". Maybe there's a reason SpaceX is doing a LEO constellation, regardless of their unfair advantages in that regard. Of course latency is an issue. Engineers will run away. Maybe you don't need them to succeed, maybe they are 0.1% of the market. Of course, where would Apple be without software engineer and designer buy in? Maybe the average customer shouldn't care, 'cause they're all high latency ok. Doesn't stop them from being swayed by marketing. A single infographic showing why low latency is better -- all else being equal -- what are customers going to choose? Not sure why YC would have invested in this other than to broaden their portfolio. The chances of this company becoming a unicorn must be vanishingly small. If unicorns are no longer the VC mantra, cool, I've got a lifestyle business you can throw money at, provided there are zero expectations. By all means prove me wrong and best of luck to you. Take this is as constructive criticism. If you're going to engage anyone in public bring your A game.
storyTitle: Astranis emerges from stealth with new satellite tech for connecting the world
outcome: Astranis raised $250 million at a $1.4 billion valuation and put its first commercial satellite into orbit.
outcomeDetail: Astranis raised a $250 million round led by BlackRock in 2021, valuing it at $1.4 billion, and has raised more than $350 million overall. Its first commercial satellite, Arcturus, launched in 2023, though a solar-array problem limited its service.
note: The comment mocked the company's chances of becoming a unicorn; it became one within three years. The technical path was harder than promised, but Astranis stayed in business and reached orbit.

author: oconnore
cardQuote: The whole notion of the powerwall is based on the assumption that either utilities or consumers are irrational.
quote: The whole notion of the powerwall is based on the assumption that either utilities or consumers are irrational. If buying a powerwall was at all economical, utilities would buy them in bulk, charge them on wholesale power, alter their pricing structure, and make a larger margin than you ever could. If powerwalls aren't economical, the only reason they make sense is to capitalize on consumers who are willing to buy the thing because its cool, or because they like living "off the grid". Utilities also have access to utility-scale energy storage -- pumped hydro, thermal, etc -- which is far cheaper than consumer focused powerwalls.
storyTitle: Tesla Powerwall: Crunching the Numbers for Australia
outcome: Tesla installed its millionth Powerwall in 2025 and turned energy storage into a multibillion-dollar business.
outcomeDetail: Powerwall moved from a 2015 niche product to a mass-market home battery, with the millionth unit installed in 2025. Tesla's energy division reported $10.1 billion in revenue in 2024, and 85,000 California Powerwalls delivered 601 MW during an October 2026 peak event.
note: oconnore's armchair economics assumed utilities would capture all storage value. Instead, homeowners bought Powerwalls in volume, and Tesla Energy became a major profit center.

author: jacobsenscott
cardQuote: I would bet a tesla roof actually reduces your house value.
quote: Assuming you'll be in the same house for 30 years is a big gamble. What if you need to move in 5 or 10 years? You're house value doesn't go up $40k when you put $40k tesla roof on top. I would bet a tesla roof actually reduces your house value. Imagine the cost of any roof maintenance, or trying to find a roofer who can work on it without just doing more damage.
storyTitle: Tesla’s new Solar Roof costs less than a new roof plus solar panels
outcome: Tesla discontinued its Solar Roof in August 2026 after installing only about 3,000 roofs since 2016.
outcomeDetail: Tesla announced the Solar Roof in 2016 and began installations in 2017, but the product never reached mass volume. By 2026 only about 3,000 roofs had been installed, and Tesla discontinued the product in August 2026, leaving installers with losses.
note: jacobsenscott's concern about resale value and maintenance was directionally right. The product was not just overpriced; it was discontinued after failing to scale.

author: philipkglass
cardQuote: I just don't think that Oklo knows what they are doing.
quote: Here's the denial letter to Oklo directly from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission: https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML2135/ML21357A034.pdf All Oklo application documents linked to from this top level page: https://www.nrc.gov/reactors/new-reactors/col/aurora-oklo.ht... While searching World Nuclear News for background about Oklo I ran into this story: "Oklo to power bitcoin mining machines" https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/Oklo-to-power-Bi... This is dubious on a couple of levels. Micro-reactors like Oklo (1.5 megawatt electrical output per unit, compared to 1000+ megawatts for Generation III reactors currently being built) would be hard pressed to produce electricity suitable for an industry that seeks globally-cheapest prices. Announcing a "20-year commercial partnership" to supply 100 units to a mining firm, before they've built a single unit, is optimistic to the point of recklessness. The Oklo founders [1], Caroline Cochran and Jacob DeWitte, have no industrial experience, according to their LinkedIn profiles. They met at MIT while TA'ing and went straight from graduate school to founding Oklo. I just don't think that Oklo knows what they are doing. [1] https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/28/oklo-planning-nuclear-micro-...
storyTitle: Nuclear startup Oklo gets thumbs-down from regulators
outcome: Oklo went public on the NYSE in 2024 and later won Air Force and data-center power deals.
outcomeDetail: Oklo listed via a SPAC merger in May 2024 and used the capital to advance its Aurora microreactor. It signed a U.S. Air Force project at Eielson AFB and power agreements with data-center customers, though its NRC combined license was still under review in 2026.
note: philipkglass's dismissal of the founders looked sharp after the NRC rejected their first application. But Oklo raised public capital, won defense customers and kept the license process alive, so 'doesn't know what they're doing' was too final.

author: sparkman55
cardQuote: These data sets turned out to be difficult to monetize
quote: Funny you should mention meteorological use cases. At a previous startup, we built global historical weather data sets (at 5km resolution, 30+ year hourly time series), accessible via a metered API. This took HPC, storage, and engineering investment about an order of magnitude less than Planet. We also had a whole room of tapes filled with satellite imagery from the world's governmental Met offices... Our main use case was for wind and solar renewable energy, but we also entertained other uses, like architecture and agriculture. These data sets turned out to be difficult to monetize; while the continental US data set may have broken even, the rest of the globe never recouped the cost of storage, let alone the supercomputer time. It's not that people around the world weren't interested in the data, they just couldn't justify paying for it.
storyTitle: Planet Labs Raises $118M Series C to Cover the Earth in Tiny Satellites
outcome: Planet went public in 2021 and now operates the largest commercial Earth-imaging fleet, though it remains unprofitable.
outcomeDetail: Planet listed on the NYSE via a SPAC in December 2021 and operates hundreds of Dove and SkySat satellites, imaging the Earth daily. Revenue grew past $200 million a year, but the company has continued to report losses.
note: sparkman55's warning about monetizing global imagery was prescient: Planet achieved scale but not durable profits. The company still became the category leader, so the dismissal was only half right.

author: aerovistae
cardQuote: I have a feeling this is yet another ooh-shiny company lacking the ability to really build something on the scale of what Tesla has done.
quote: They have a cool logo and I'm all for further progress in this field and hope the best, but I have a feeling this is yet another ooh-shiny company lacking the ability to really build something on the scale of what Tesla has done. The fact that the lead designer built the i3 doesn't bode well either.
storyTitle: New Electric Car Company Emerges: Faraday Future
outcome: Faraday Future delivered only a handful of cars and its shares collapsed.
outcomeDetail: Faraday Future unveiled the FF 91 in 2017 but repeatedly delayed production. It began deliveries in 2023 and had delivered only a small number of vehicles by 2025, while its stock fell to penny-stock levels and the company pivoted to a lower-priced brand.
note: aerovistae's 'ooh-shiny company' read was right. Faraday Future raised and burned billions without ever building at Tesla's scale, and its production never amounted to more than a token run.

author: sh87
cardQuote: Their chief "strategy" officer promises cheap vehicles even if battery prices don’t continue to fall by setting up "microfactories".
quote: Their chief "strategy" officer promises cheap vehicles even if battery prices don’t continue to fall by setting up "microfactories". This reminded me of a project I knew from 2016, whose pitch to management was cheaper running costs by splitting a monolithic application into microservices. That did not go well neither for the team, nor management.
storyTitle: Hyundai and Kia back Arrival, a British startup making electric delivery vans
outcome: Arrival entered administration in 2024 without producing its electric vans at scale.
outcomeDetail: Arrival went public at a $5.4 billion valuation in 2021 and promised microfactories near customers. It never reached volume production; its UK arm entered administration in February 2024 and its assets were auctioned off.
note: sh87 mocked the microfactory pitch by comparing it to a failed microservices reorg, and the analogy held. Arrival's distributed-manufacturing model ran out of cash before it could prove unit economics.

author: credit_guy
cardQuote: Fusion is N years in the future and it will always be so. N=30. With the news from Commonwealth Fusion Systems, N is still 30.
quote: Fusion is N years in the future and it will always be so. N=30. With the news from Commonwealth Fusion Systems, N is still 30. And it will keep being 30 for a while. Why? People are averse to radioactivity. Fusion produces a huge amount of neutrons, and those neutrons transmute the nuclei they encounter and result in radioactive waste. If you decide you can put up with radioactive waste, you might as well use fission. For other disadvantages of fusion, you can check [1]. Where fusion can shine is in fusion-fission hybrid reactors [2]. This can not only be used for energy generation, but also to dispose of the accumulated nuclear waste. [1] https://thebulletin.org/2017/04/fusion-reactors-not-what-the... [2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion%E2%80%93fission...
storyTitle: Fusion startup plans reactor with small but powerful superconducting magnets
outcome: CFS raised $1.8 billion, demonstrated a 20-tesla magnet and signed a Google power deal, but SPARC first plasma slipped to 2027.
outcomeDetail: Commonwealth Fusion Systems closed a $1.8 billion Series B in 2021 and later added $863 million from Google, Nvidia and others. It built a record 20-tesla high-temperature superconducting magnet and signed a Google offtake agreement, but SPARC's first plasma and net-energy demonstration slipped to 2027.
note: credit_guy was right that commercial fusion keeps slipping, and SPARC did slip again. But 'N is still 30' understated how much capital and real hardware CFS assembled; the company became the leading private fusion bet.

author: the_duke
cardQuote: Combine that with limited speed and range, and I just don't see the concept taking off in a big way.
quote: There are a lot of companies working on "flying taxis". All of those seem to have a large footprint with lots of rotors, meaning they will need dedicated landing/take off zones. This seems to limit their usability a lot, turning them more into a short range point to point helicopter service. Not to mention the noise pollution. Those things are all loud. Combine that with limited speed and range, and I just don't see the concept taking off in a big way. Some other competitors: * Volocopter: https://www.volocopter.com https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OazFiIhwAEs * Hyunday S-A1: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L6K7GAG1Aas * Bell Nexus: https://www.bellflight.com/products/bell-nexus * Ehang: https://www.ehang.com/ehang184/index https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d66MoI4GdFs * Kitty Hawk HeavySide (Larry Page pet project): https://kittyhawk.aero https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q7mc3C19kE4 * Lilium (branded as jet): https://lilium.com https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qotuu8JjQM
storyTitle: Toyota invests $394m in Joby Aviation's flying taxis
outcome: Joby went public in 2021, raised billions and began flying air-taxi demonstrations in New York and Dubai.
outcomeDetail: Joby listed via a SPAC in August 2021 and has raised more than $3 billion, including nearly $900 million from Toyota. By 2026 it was flying demonstration flights in Dubai and New York and targeting its first paying passengers, though commercial scale remained unproven.
note: the_duke was right that eVTOLs are noisy, short-range helicopter replacements, not mass transit. But the concept did take off: Joby flew demonstrator aircraft, built vertiports and moved toward passenger launch.

author: baybal2
cardQuote: Well, they do that 3D printing thing. I do not believe this delivering much of economic gain.
quote: Well, they do that 3D printing thing. I do not believe this delivering much of economic gain.
storyTitle: Relativity Space raises $35M for a new process to build and fly rockets
outcome: Relativity raised $1.3 billion at a $4.2 billion valuation and flew the first 3D-printed rocket to space in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Relativity's Terran 1 launched in March 2023 and became the first mostly 3D-printed rocket to reach space, though its upper stage failed before orbit. The company retired Terran 1 and pivoted to the larger Terran R, while its valuation reached $4.2 billion in 2021.
note: baybal2 was skeptical that 3D printing would deliver economic gains, and Terran 1 never reached orbit. But the company raised over $1 billion and proved the manufacturing approach could fly, so the flat dismissal was too early.

author: jonknee
cardQuote: In my opinion it's actually a lot more likely that Tesla goes bankrupt and it becomes a solely Panasonic factory than it does a solely Tesla factory.
quote: Well Panasonic literally owns big parts of the factory (and will be the ones making the batteries!). They are going to be partners for a very long time. In my opinion it's actually a lot more likely that Tesla goes bankrupt and it becomes a solely Panasonic factory than it does a solely Tesla factory.
outcome: The Gigafactory became one of the world's largest battery plants, and Tesla did not go bankrupt.
outcomeDetail: Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory began cell production with Panasonic in 2016 and grew into one of the largest battery factories on earth. Tesla survived its Model 3 cash crunch, became the world's most valuable automaker, and later added in-house cell manufacturing.
note: jonknee's bankruptcy prediction was specific and wrong. Panasonic remained a partner, but the factory became a Tesla asset and a core part of its cost advantage, not a Panasonic takeover.
